9.title: great father/daughter movie for scientists/engineers
9.content:
Thank you, Christopher Nolan, for bringing another great science-based father/daughter movie into being. As an engineer with a pre-teenage daughter, I am grateful to have wonderfully entertaining films like Interstellar and Contact with which, for a brief time, I can pull my little one away from her literary world of magic and Greek gods and into my world of science and technology.

It did not feel like a three hour movie. At no point was I not completely involved in what was unfolding in front of me. To make a long film hold the audience's interest, director Nolan and composer Zimmer have done an outstanding job. I had read that the soundtrack was too loud and covered up much dialog. I did not find that to be the case, and I am hard of hearing.

Jessica Chastain (adult Murph) was not believable to me as a scientist. I work surrounded by engineers and scientists, and they rarely display uninhibited emotion. Instead, you see a lot more thinking going in their eyes when they are conversing -- sort of like they are occasionally looking away at a computer screen. Hollywood actors really need to do some on-site research with mathematicians and physicists before taking on a role like this. Jody Foster did a much more believable job as a scientist in "Contact". Mackenzie Foy (as young Murph) was better than Chastain, but still lacked some of the credibility of Jena Malone (young Ellie Arroway) in Contact.

There were the usual scientific problems with the film, but most of that can be forgiven. They did get a lot of it right, and it was gratifying to have the issues of relative time and gravity dealt with in a film for the mass audience. Most importantly for me, I had assumed that the premise of the Earth's demise as a life-sustaining planet would be blamed on overpopulation, overconsumption, or the latest bugaboo, Global Warming. It was not. And, to top off that last slight to pseudo-science, the only evil character in the film was obviously meant to ridicule Michael Mann (of the infamous "Hockey Stick" temperature chart). Dr Mann (the character) has to convince Earth's scientists that his frozen planet is actually warm, or otherwise he will be left there for eternity. The real Dr Mann has to convince Earth's politicians that our planet is warming, or otherwise he will be left in obscurity. A laugh-out-loud moment for me during the film.

9.title: Great Movie
9.content:
Directed by Christopher Nolan, Interstellar was a fantastic movie that encompassed everything from a second Dust Bowl to physics to space exploration. The plot of the story was a little hard to follow and towards the tail end of the film became extremely confusing. The movie begins by vaguely explaining that the world has suffered another Dust Bowl, resulting in limited food and resources. The conditions got so bad in the movie, the characters were forced to wear protective goggles, cover their mouths, and set plates/cups upside down to prevent dust intake. Thus, propelling the movie forward. The dusts implications were large as crops such as wheat and okra have become extinct with corn as one of the last remaining sources of food. As the story continues we come across a secret organization (NASA) working on saving civilization through space exploration and the theory of harnessing gravity to ensure the human race would survive, just on a different planet. In order to not completely spoil the movie, I recommend everyone watch Interstellar and see what events ensue, as it is a great movie!

In addition, I believe it is necessary to analyze the believability of the initial 30 minutes of the movie as it touches on a climate related topic/potential issue. A second Dust Bowl, as detailed in Interstellar, is completely plausible in today's environment due to increases in global temperatures as well as extended droughts throughout parts of the world. The mass extinction of individual crops could be a consequence of additional dust bowls and simultaneously result in minimal future food resources. The ramifications of an additional Dust Bowl/s could be parallel to the first Dust Bowl in the United States' Midwest or even similar to the one portrayed in Interstellar. No matter the case, Nolan's depiction of the Dust Bowl is accurate and is a real-life event that should be avoided. People in the movie failed to learn in time the consequences of global climate change and were forced to leave Earth or perish after exhausting all of Earth's resources. So, what can be done to limit a second Dust Bowl? And what should have been done in Interstellar? The answer to both of these questions are the same, limit the burning of fossil fuels (prevent the continued warming of the atmosphere) and erect policy for tackling the issue of climate change (industrial activity, development, etc.). However, in order to complete these tasks all countries must be on the same page. Meaning every government recognizes the issue and agrees to work towards fixing the problem in order to save our plant and most importantly the Human race.

9.title: A must-see space drama film. Much better in IMAX.
9.content:
"I'm not afraid of death. ... I'm afraid of time."

Space and time. Faith and science. Complacency and proactivity. Lie and sacrifice. Reality and artistic depiction.

---

Imagine making time the antagonist of your film. Christopher Nolan takes you through a mesmerizing cosmic dance of space and time bearing witness to humanity's best and worst instincts for survival. With an IMAX Digital 4K projector on a gigantic screen that quite literally covers an entire wall and a 12-channel sound system that can mimic the rumblings of a spacecraft traversing an incomprehensible dimension inside the theater accompanied by a score by Hans Zimmer produced mainly with a church organ, the film transports you to a barren yet hypnotizingly beautiful landscape near a supermassive black hole where you find yourself rolling a die on the fate of the human species. There's ethical and philosophical questions about what it means to be a sacrifice and the lengths one can or should go to survive. Throughout all this, the film somehow manages to keep a focus on the humanity and the human scale of time.

You can criticize it for the several artistic liberties they've taken to craft a story but I feel a lot of it is justified except maybe for the very last scene which is slightly debatable imho. Even then, I can understand that they were just trying to tie a narrative thread at the very end. It's a leap of faith--a suspension of disbelief.

This is the greatest cinematic experience I've ever had in my life. It's crafted specifically for IMAX and is meant to be experienced in an IMAX theater. I can't even imagine what the true best IMAX experience with 70 mm film at the approximate resolution of 18K would be like.

9.title: Interstellar: an Astronomical Success
9.content:
Interstellar is one of the best films of 2014, despite its immense run time of 2 hours and 49 minutes. Interstellar is a Science Fiction drama. The movie really shows the Emptiness of space. The movie is directed by Christopher Nolan and scored by Hans Zimmer. The premise of the movie is plant life on earth is dying because the crops got infected with Blight and the massive death of crops has sent the whole world into a dust bowl, so humanity must colonize other planets in order to survive. The main character Cooper, who is played by Matthew McConaughey must pilot his ship through space with the help of Dr. Brand, played by Anne Hathaway and T.A.R.S. The military robot, played by Bill Irwin, to colonize another planet so the human race can continue living. This film features many good cast members such as Matt Damon, Casey Affleck, and Jessica Chastain. This entire movie is good and most of the science in the movie makes sense in it too.

Interstellar is one of the most stunning visually and emotional films of 2014. The film is directed by Christopher Nolan, Nolan has made many other good films such as Dunkirk, Memento, The Dark Knight Trilogy, and Inception, all of these films are visually stunning. One scene in particular was rather Awe-Inspiring, there is a moment when they are on a planet with massive waves and with the angles that capture the waves at their fullest and really show the danger of the situation that the astronauts are in. The visuals are amazing and Christopher Nolan really delivers, you can tell that he is experienced in capturing incredible shots especially with his past movies like Inception where he folds a town in half. This movie shows the talent of Christopher Nolan fully and leaves me awe-struck at the end.

The film also sounds amazing and features the musical talents of Hans Zimmer, who has been featured in Inception, Gladiator, Dunkirk, and The Dark Knight Trilogy. Hans Zimmer has been known to deliver and leave thrilling Soundtracks throughout all the movies that he produces. As for and Interstellar this is no exception, throughout the movie he builds up the music making it more and more intense and emotional for the audience and he releases all of his talent in the song No Time For Caution, this scene had me on the edge of my seat, the camera was spinning all and focused on the spaceship, the camera matching its rotation while the music is building extreme tension for the audience. Hans Zimmer demonstrates his talent of making music that builds the scene up and allows it to become the best scene it can possibly be. It's hard to make a good movie without a good soundtrack and Hans Zimmer delivers it through the piano and violins throughout the movie. This Soundtrack is breathtaking and had me at the edge of my seat holding my breath when Hans needed to build suspense.

Matthew McConaughey was the main character and he was not the right person for this movie, he plays the dad and ex-pilot character of Cooper very well but the audience is sidetracked often because he is very quiet over the entire movie making it difficult to follow. This speaks more to the acting of Matthew rather than the Directing of Christopher Nolan. Instead it would have made more sense for Matt Damon, Paul Rudd, or even Casey Affleck as the main character of this movie. I believe this movie would have been even more successful and Emotional with these actors playing Cooper instead of Matthew McConaughey.

Lastly, Interstellar is one of my favorite movies of all time due to the visuals that are in this Science Fiction Drama. The movie as a whole is very long and manages to stay interesting and powerful to the audience due to the Soundtrack and Visual effects brought on by the Captivating Christopher Nolan. This movie is very emotional and the raw emotion that Cooper gives towards the end of the movie resonates through the audience. Christopher Nolan and Hans Zimmer Really delivered an amazing movie and I was left speechless at the end of it, truly a science fiction masterpiece.

9.title: Heil Hathaway- Spoilers
9.content:
I wonder about the number of decisions that go into making a movie as epic and complex as Interstellar. I cannot even imagine how many choices have to be made about the script, the cast, the special effects, the editing, the score, and countless behind the scenes moves. So I understand that you cannot get every decision right. But who OK'd giving Anne Hathaway the exact same haircut as Adolph Hitler? Interstellar is an admirable movie: smart, ambitious, innovative, with a compelling story, believable leading performances, and incredible special effects. But every time Herr Hathaway was on-screen (and she is the second lead), I was worried she was going to use the rifts in space-time to zip back to 1939 and invade Poland.

Interstellar takes place in the near future, after a blight has destroyed much of the world's food supply. Only corn is currently immune from the blight but it's future is looking shaky. Dust storms ravage the American heartland and most of the people who survived the famine are required to farm. The current generation considers itself a caretaker generation, managing the decline without any hope for the future.

All except for reluctant farmer, former test pilot, and all around good guy Matthew Mccoughney's Coop. Coop is not content to grow corn, drink beers on the porch with his father (father-in-law, maybe...either way played by John Lithgow). Coop dreams of solving the problems of the world. I forget exactly how because I was a little bit stoned for the first hour of this movie, but somehow Coop meets up with secret NASA (something to do with a beacon and a pick-up truck and finally some X-Filesy looking chain link fence enclosed buildings). Times have been so tough for NASA they have had to get a foreigner to run them, but luckily for them that foreigner is Michael Caine. Michael Caine, whose working-class London accent has never left him, is a mathematical genius trying to figure out something about black holes with one of those huge chalkboards filled with one equation like in movies or cartoons. Good to know that even in the near apocalyptic future we may not be able to grow wheat, but we still have the cliches of a New Yorker cartoon.

They send Coop up to visit other planets to check on the prior settlers who were sent to find a substitute for earth. Because this is a Christopher Nolan movie, every planet and adventure has some weird time component. So an hour on the tidal wave planet is actually 27 years for the spaceship circling the tidal wave planet. Smartly, they left the black guy in the spaceship, so after an hour at the beach for Coop and Reichsfurher Hathaway and 27 years for their black crewmate, all three look the same age (black don't crack!). Then the next planet has Matt Damon (I guess he comes with the Goodwill Hunting style equations on chalkboards), whose planet is totally uninhabitable, but he lied so they would come rescue him.

Coop finally sacrifices himself for Heil Hathaway and gets sucked into a blackhole. In the blackhole is the back of his daughter's bookcase, which, I am guessing, is not astronomically accurate. In any case, Coop is able to use morse code messages by pushing books off the shelf to give his now grown daughter (Jessica Chastain) the information she needs to complete Michael Caine's equation. The guy from Failure to Launch crashes a spaceship in blackhole but is then able to use the technique from the first scene in Ghostbusters to solve the most complex equation in history. If you are looking for cinema verite you will have to look elsewhere.

The new equation works, Jessica Chastain (now old and played by Ellen Burstyn) saves the day and gets humanity relocated to some moon of Jupiter. Which seems awfully close since Coop and Anne Hilteraway were traveling through wormholes and light years; comparatively the moons of Jupiter are next door. Coop sees his daughter just before she dies, and then heads back out in the cosmos find hottie-space-Hitler who is stranded on some other planet (again, echoing Goodwill Hunting's final scene, but with a spaceship instead of an '87 Caprice).

The movie is ambitious. I wonder how much of this movie is Christopher Nolan feeling like Coop, looking at the mediocre movies being made and wanting to do more? The special effects are great, and the cast is excellent (though heartthrob Timothee Chalamet's character ages into Casey Affleck (another Goodwill Hunting reference); I think if Chalamet knew that was going to happen he would have rooted for the blight). The movie is too long (I had to watch in two sittings, which I normally dislike. But that is why I was a little stoned for the first half, but not the second), has a plot that does not really make sense, and is absolutely in love with the concept of time being relative. And time is relative. But I don't think it is relative vis-a-vis two people on a plant vs the guy circling 5 miles up on the ship. When the astronauts come back from the International Space Station we don't all marvel at how they have aged 27 years in our three earth hours. But one does not watch Matthew Mccoughney movies for an accurate portrayal of relativity. Dazed and Confused didn't explain quantum mechanics, but I would still recommend it.

No director has the ambition, the money, and the talent to make movies like this other than Nolan. His movies don't always work, but they are never boring. I wish I had seen Interstellar in a theater, as it was intended to be seen. Would that more of Hollywood reached for the stars, instead ofgrowing corn here on earth.

9.title: Been putting this one off for years due to my skepticism
9.content:
If you were to ask someone to choose a film from 2014, chances are that Interstellar would be a film that they would choose. Interstellar was a big deal upon release in 2014 and for me (as a 12 year old) I remember all the praise that I heard about this film but I never had gotten the chance to watch it. Why? Because I was actually really skeptical over this film. It was until a friend basically said that I should watch it that I finally gave in. Interstellar was directed by Christopher Nolan (Inception and the Dark Knight films) and stars a whole bunch of people including Matthew McConaughey (Dazed and Confused), Anne Hathaway (Les Mis), and Jessica Chastain (It Chapter Two). Again, all of which is to name a few. The film was a critical success and also a financial success, making it the 10th highest grossing film of 2014. Funny enough, as I was writing this review, I found out that there is an unofficial Russian-Ukrainian sequel called Interstelar 2: Operation Terra 2040. Funny.........

The film takes place in a dystopian type of Earth where space travel is mostly forgotten to the point that the moon landing was deemed, fake. A farmer named Cooper and his daughter accidentally come across NASA and they recruit Cooper on a mission. Apparently the Earth will be destroyed by famine in a short time and the only possible way is to take a team (including Cooper) through a black hole where there are possible Earth 2's to bring the humans to. It is a risk Cooper is gonna have to take, even if it means being away from his family.

Interstellar is a good film. A great film too. I have seen some of the complaints about this film and it seems fitting that I address these complaints and see where my stance is on them. First, is the length of the film. Personally, I do not mind a film being this long as long as what the film is is a great experience. Interstellar is a great experience. If anything, the film should not be shortened due to it's length but rather shortened due to some extraneous scenes. The film can be split into three parts. The second third of the film is were the largely extraneous bits are and I cannot go more in depth unless I want to have a review with spoilers and I do not want that. Honestly, that would be my only complaint about the film hence the nine star rating and not the ten star rating that I nearly gave this film. With that being said, I have seen the complaints centered around the science-ey stuff and whatnot and that is something that might get some people. For me though, I found it pretty straightforward for the most part and if something did not make sense to me at first, it eventually did. I am certaint that I only grasp the mere basics of the film and not all of the things about the relativity and what not, but as long as one has the basics, it should all be fine. For those who are more intellectual might have a blast with this film too. Yes, there is a lot of explaining but for a film like this, I think if there was a lack of explaining, the film would be bad. That is pretty much all of the criticisms that I have heard from others and all of which are very valid points. The positives are far greater than the negatives (obviously). The visuals was something that has been constantly praised and it is not hard to see why. The special effects are great and it is as if they actually filmed this in space. It was that good. The acting is great and so was the directing here. Christopher Nolan is just that good. This film can be easily compared to 2001: A Space Odyssey. For me, 2001 is the better film. What I am trying to say is that there is a sort of similarities between the two. The film has it's emotional moments which are really effective.

Interstellar is a great film. I am sure people have minor problems with this film and it is not hard to see why. But if you just decide to turn off your brain and sit back and relax and watch the show, you will be entertained.

9.title: Excellent film, but fails to reach its true potential
9.content:
This movie really gets a lot of things right. It's meticulously directed, acted and scored and has some of the most believable awe-inspiring visual effects ever seen in a sci-fi. That's why it is such a shame that the script fails to carry this incredible high through all the way to the end. Specifically when launched into the final act of the film, the previously superb storytelling gives away to unnecessary exposition. Instead of entrusting the audience with the task to ponder the ending and make up their own mind about what really happened (which would have benefited the movie greatly), Nolan introduces a forced cheesy plot-element that even contradicts the scientific realism displayed earlier in the movie.

I would urge everyone to go see Interstellar, because despite its flaws it is undeniably a great piece of filmmaking. Unfortunately though, I cannot say that I consider it a true masterpiece.

9.title: An epic, the most beautiful film about humanity ever made
9.content:
Cooper's haunted looks sear through. He looks so alone. Out cold inside a black hole, he yearns, and remembers. It is his daughter--back on Earth that he had left with a promise. A promise he now knows he can't keep. He has failed.

**************************************************

This is a film not just about parenthood. It is anthropological in its canvas. Humankind is struggling to survive, and we see all of our species' defining features here. It is about humanity's best and worst. 'Mann' lies to ensure his survival. Cooper braves a black hole to send Brand on her way, wryly quoting the Newton's third law, "The only way humans have ever figured out of getting somewhere is to leave something behind." Brand still loves someone who she hasn't seen in decades, and is pulled light years towards him. We may be three dimensional beings, but 'love is the one thing we're capable of perceiving that transcends dimensions of time and space.' For a moment, I am reminded of 'The Dark Knight Rises' when Mann says, "Our survival instinct is our single greatest source of inspiration." The film seems to be an ode to Murphy's law--whatever that can happen will happen—as almost every single thing that could have gone wrong with the mission goes wrong; and to the Darwin's law of adaptability, when Cooper and Brand adapt to the ever increasing complexities of their mission to stay alive.

"Once you're a parent, you're the ghost of your children's future."

Cooper's predicament is universal. He chooses 'not' to be merely a ghost. He rises above his immediate goals in favor of his future ones. He wonders. He plans. Thus he achieves.

"Nature is not evil."

Cooper boldly goes where no one has ever gone before--inside the singularity. For him, Murphy's law is not a pessimistic take on nature, it is about fairness. That is why he does not give up hope for the future of Earth's remaining inhabitants, and vaults into the 'gentle' singularity of the black hole, even though he had no way of relaying the quantum information just yet.

"Rage, rage against the dying of the light."

Dylan Thomas' famous poem is heard reverberating throughout. And that is how the action goes. Every character, even Tom fights to save the crop he grew. Cooper docks into a wildly spinning Endurance defying everyone around him, because he just couldn't give up. Humanity fights hard to survive across galaxies, as time watches.

"I'm not afraid of death..., I'm afraid of time."

Cooper's primary struggle is against time. He wants to save the future. He is left maimed by relativity, but he continues on, not caring for the costs. He is haunted by his memories, but he manages not to become one himself.

****************************************

Cooper's survival instincts kick in. He realizes the time tesseract is not a prison, but a gateway to peer into time. He watches his daughter stare forlornly towards the bookcase. Can he communicate with her in time? The harder he tries, the bitter the results are. He sees himself walking out the door, leaving her bundled up in her fury. He realizes what he has to do. Humanity was born on Earth, but it was never to meant to die there. And so it shall be.

Interstellar like many sci-fi epics ends up raising more questions than it answers.The following interpretation manages to answer MOST OF THEM.

Here goes. |Spoilers Ahead|

Humanity has survived The Blight somehow, and have evolved into highly intellectual species who understood how to transcend information through time.

These evolved-humans can be correlated with the so called 'they' who have been referred far too many times in the movie. Their sole mission is to make sure that Plan A is successful and humanity with as many people possible survive the disaster. They use Cooper in particular to help solve the Plan A, hence the singularity is shown in that specific manner, also once the passage of information using gravity is done the 'Tesseract' is destroyed since its purpose is served.

This explains the positioning of wormhole near Saturn and also the 'Tesseract' inside the Gargantua (Black Hole). Now how in the hell did cooper travel from singularity to our solar system beats me but it sure makes for a good ending.

Meanwhile on Earth Murph decodes the information given by her father and solves the equation put forth by Brand, which helps them to manipulate gravity and invent Cooper-Station, Using which humanity survives. In the end Cooper after his meeting with Murph uses the wormhole again to go after Amelia, who is stuck on Edmund's planet which turns out to be the only habitable planet on the other side. 9.title: That human spirit and a love that transcends space and time
9.content:
I caught Interstellar probably in the last week it was in the theaters here. Glad I did, it was a very well done movie that made you think about many things, like: 1) What happens if the world you've come to expect to be there for humans suddenly is ending. 2) Can the human spirit and love transcend time and space 3) Can we as a human race survive in another galaxy on other planets and continue to evolve.

What I liked most about Interstellar was that even though it was a sci-fi story it had a real interesting story-line. I think that's what made it better for me than Gravity. Gravity was about space travel too, but its story-line lacked that human element. Interstellar is more like Dune, one of the great sci-fi movies. It had a real story attached to it.

I went to see Interstellar, because of a posting on twitter by Sam Heughan about love. I didn't know what he was implying when he posted that very thoughtful comment after he saw it. I understood it once I saw it. The underlying theme of the story was about a father and daughter's love for each other, that human spirit, that emotion that drives man kind to be greater than they are for each other. That kind of love that can transcends time and space as another dimension that humans share.

Well acted by Matthew McConaughey (Cooper) who once again proves his acting abilities are top notch and by relatively new comer Mackenzie Foy (Murph) who steals the show with a memorable performance as his daughter. Other notables in the film: Anne Hathaway does a wonderful job as a scientist who goes on the voyage with Matthew; Michael Caine still able to deliver a meaningful performance as Anne's father who dupes them into going on this mission knowing they will not be able to return. A choice he makes to save mankind. Jessica Chastain as the adult Murph who does finally figure out how to save the people on earth. Matt Damon playing a relatively minor role as the villain that almost ends the mission out of human self interest. Others as well with minor roles all add to the believable story-line.

One of the best sci-fi movies I've seen in a long time. Really enjoyed it.

9.title: Not Nolan's Best, But Still A Very Enjoyable Film
9.content:
Interstellar is directed by the one and only Christopher Nolan, and stars Matthew Mcconaughey as Cooper, an ex-pilot in a futuristic Earth, where another Dust Bowl has taken place, and Earth is no longer a suitable home for the human race. One day, Cooper and his daughter Murphy (Murph, for short) stumble upon NASA's base, who was long thought gone, and Cooper is recruited to lead a team through a wormhole next to Saturn, so that humans could colonize a different planet, and live on. Oh, and Anne Hathaway is in there, too.

To start, the movie's directed by Nolan, so of course it's beautifully directed, and is one of the best looking movies I've ever seen, in terms of cinematography. All of the full screen shots of different planets, and black holes, and such look completely amazing. The score is also great (thanks Hans Zimmer). Every time anything was happening, the pounding score just sucked you right into the situation.

The acting was also top notch. Matthew Mcconaughey does great as Cooper, and you really feel for him having to leave his family, particularly his daughter Murph, and the emotional impact that has on him. Anne Hathaway does great as well, although she has a pretty shallow character. Jessica Chastain does great as Murph, also portraying the emotional connection between Murph and Cooper. The whole cast do well in their roles. However, this leads into the first big negative.

The characters are very washed out, and lead to a script that's too long. Casey Affleck plays Cooper's son, and his character is completely unnecessary. This character even causes a sub plot towards the end of the film, that probably adds 10 to 15 minutes to the run time. Another tacked on character would be Dr. Mann, played by Matt Damon. He obviously symbolizes mankind, and adds around 25 minutes to the film with his subplot. Overall, this movie is near three hours, mostly due to all of these subplots.

Another predictable and tacked on thing is a plot twist that occurs toward the end, dealing with Murph's "ghost." There really wasn't much need for this, and it felt very unnecessary.

Now, in conclusion, is this Nolan's best film? No. Definitely not. However, I'm not saying it's bad. It really is quite good, in all reality. I'm going to give Interstellar an A-, or a 9 out of 10.

9.title: Imaginative and Real Science Fiction
9.content:
A wonderful, imaginative, and finally real sci-fi premise takes us on a journey to the outer-limits of imagination. Very Imaginative yet keeping within the realms of real science fiction as opposed to fantasy, Interstellar may be what Sci-Fi people have been waiting for since 2001 A Space Odyssey. Interstellar, undeniably influenced by 2001, will likely join 2001 within the pantheon of the greatest sci-fi epics ever made.

The film goes on an exciting journey though space to explore other worlds and reaches other dimensions. This premise and story line paired with the big budget extravaganza of wondrous visuals and state of the art effects make for an amazing movie going experience.

Attempting to connect this Sci-Fi with mass appeal as opposed to challenging us with novelty as Kubrick did, make Interstellar fall slightly short of that most legendary sci-fi film - 2001. For example, the wonder and amazement of the unknown of space travel will be fused with thriller/action sequences and characters that suddenly and implausibly become evil bad guys, so that the awe and amazement stemming from the unknown of space/time travel alas merge into the more routine, "entertaining", unrealistic Hollywood thrill rides with its loud music and edge of your seat, fake scenes. Fortunately those sequences are only a small, ignorable part of the grandiose film.

The wonders of space and imagination simply needed to stay within that theme to capture the audience; instead these wonders become diminished by implementing Hollywood drama and emotions expressed by the astronauts chosen to embark on the mission. Feeling a bit miscast, when seeing Ann Hathaway (who plays one of the astronauts) putting on her singing in Les Miserable face, also Matt Damon, and even Mathew McConaughey (despite decent acting from him), led the mesmerizing journey into the unknowns of our universe(successfully accomplished in 2001, where its sterility from its astronauts made the actual outer-space become more of the character), to a mood that is a bit more ordinary and mainstream than some may hope for. I guess I personally wished for a slightly different film, one that didn't need to dwell as much on the human emotional world and chose to be where the setting actually was in outer space. A film explaining a bit more about the scientific phenomenon going on in planet earth that led to the need to seek out habitable planets and more explanations of what is going on in space. By the conclusion, there was a typical Nolanesque, mind bending, brain twisting conclusion challenging the audience to decipher what happened. The truth is the conclusion might be genius and really work brilliantly if it is able to be correctly understood or it might be something meant to be subject to interpretation.

These tarnishes could not hold back the film from reaching and attaining those outer-limits. Since the premise and story were undeniably there and visually we were exposed to the imagination of the wonders and awe of space, time and other dimensions.

9.title: great movie
9.content:
Interstellar is a science fiction movie directed by Christopher Nolan and released in 2014. The film features a star-studded cast including Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, and Jessica Chastain, among others. The movie follows a group of astronauts who travel through a wormhole in search of a new home for humanity after Earth becomes uninhabitable.

Overall, Interstellar is a visually stunning and thought-provoking movie that blends science fiction with emotion and personal relationships. The cinematography is breathtaking, with stunning shots of outer space and distant planets. The special effects are also impressive, with the wormhole and black hole sequences being particularly striking.

The plot is complex and requires the audience to pay close attention, but it is well worth the effort. The themes of the movie, including the importance of science, the nature of time, and the value of human connection, are explored in a deep and meaningful way. The relationship between McConaughey's character and his daughter, played by Mackenzie Foy and later Chastain, is particularly poignant and serves as a powerful emotional anchor for the film.

9.title: "Interstellar" is the "2001:Space Odyssey" of this generation.
9.content:
Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" is an emotional and fascinating look into the future of humanity, a time when Earth's resources are scarce, corn holds the economy together, and dangerous dust clouds threaten civilians on a day to day basis. It is clear that we cannot hold out for much longer.

"You're daughter's generation will be the last...." says Professor Brand, played by Michael Caine.

The daughter in question is young Murph, played at different ages by Makenzie Foy, Jessica Chastain, and another famous actress who's name I will not reveal. Murph's father is Cooper, played with surprising sincerity by Matthew McConaughey, fresh off his Oscar win from "Dallas Buyer's Club" and proving that Wooderson finally got over his high school nostalgia and decided to grow up.

Cooper is recruited by Professor Brand to pilot a space station to the planet Saturn, where an alien wormhole has been detected. Three other expeditions have already gone through the wormhole in search of other planets that may be habitable to us. Now it's up to Cooper and his team, among them Professor Brand's own daughter played by Anne Hathaway, to zip across the galaxy and assess which of the three expeditions found the best home for the future of mankind.

The space adventure is completely spellbinding. From the launch off Earth, the journey to Saturn, the trip down the wormhole, to the unexplored worlds, and eventually into a black hole, we are given one dazzling sequence after another, showing off the vastness and beauty of the universe as the audience is invited not just to witness, but also feel as though we part of the crew. The physical science piles itself on thickly, but always assumes the audience is smart enough to know what the characters are talking about. A weaker movie would probably dumb the dialogue down, but "Interstellar" respects the intelligence of it's audience more than the average film. Several times, we feel like we're figuring things out along with the crew, especially in a spectacular sequence towards the end when McConaughey discovers certain revelations, and we are exactly one step ahead of him, sharing in the excitement.

But beyond the spectacular whimsy this film offers, it's also strongly grounded in its themes of love, separation, abandonment, fear of time, and hope for the future. It knows that doing the right thing is a complex issue. Even good people usually act on self interest. When Cooper is faced with the choice of saving the world or never seeing his daughter again, we understand where he's coming from. "Interstellar" is not the first film to send an astronaut crew into the realms of deep space to solve some sort of earthly dilemma and encounter hostile obstacles along the way. But it may be one of the best.

9.title: What a Film
9.content:
Watching Interstellar was nothing short of an extraordinary journey that left me in awe long after the credits rolled. Directed by Christopher Nolan, this film transcends the boundaries of conventional cinema, taking us on a profound voyage through space and time that is as visually stunning as it is intellectually stimulating.

From the moment Interstellar begins, you are thrust into a future Earth on the brink of ecological collapse. The desperation and urgency are palpable, setting the stage for an epic quest to save humanity. What struck me immediately was the film's ability to blend grandiose science fiction with deeply personal storytelling. The relationship between Cooper, played masterfully by Matthew McConaughey, and his daughter Murph is the emotional heart of the film, grounding the cosmic adventure in a relatable human experience.

The visuals in Interstellar are nothing short of breathtaking. Nolan and his team have created a universe that feels both vast and intimate, filled with awe-inspiring imagery that ranges from the serene beauty of distant planets to the haunting isolation of space. The scenes involving the wormhole and black hole, in particular, are mesmerizing and showcase some of the best visual effects I've ever seen. These moments are not just eye candy; they are integral to the story, making the science of the film accessible and thrilling.

Hans Zimmer's score is another standout element that elevates Interstellar to a whole new level. The music is powerful and haunting, perfectly complementing the film's themes of exploration and sacrifice. Zimmer's use of the organ adds a unique, almost spiritual dimension to the soundtrack, making certain scenes resonate even more deeply.

What makes Interstellar truly exceptional is its ambitious exploration of complex scientific concepts. Nolan doesn't shy away from diving into theories of relativity, time dilation, and the potential of other dimensions. Yet, he presents these ideas in a way that is engaging and understandable, even for those who might not be well-versed in astrophysics. The collaboration with physicist Kip Thorne ensures that the science is as accurate as it is fascinating, adding a layer of authenticity to the film.

The performances are stellar across the board. McConaughey delivers one of his finest performances, bringing depth and vulnerability to Cooper's character. Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, and Michael Caine also shine, each contributing to the film's emotional and narrative complexity. Their performances ensure that, amidst the vastness of space, the story remains intimately human.

Interstellar is more than just a sci-fi epic; it's a meditation on love, sacrifice, and the enduring human spirit. It challenges you to think about our place in the universe and the lengths we will go to protect those we love. The film's ending, which I won't spoil here, is both thought-provoking and deeply moving, leaving you with plenty to ponder.

Interstellar is a cinematic triumph that combines stunning visuals, a powerful score, and an emotionally charged story to create an unforgettable experience. It's a film that speaks to both the heart and the mind, offering a journey that is as much about the exploration of space as it is about the exploration of human connections. Whether you're a fan of science fiction or simply love great storytelling, Interstellar is a must-watch that will leave you inspired and in awe of the possibilities that lie beyond our world.

9.title: The Modern Day 2001
9.content:
Amazing Film.

I absolutely love this movie. It is one of my favorite movies of all time. I will be honest that prior to this most recent viewing I saw this movie as a masterpiece and perfect example of cinema. Now, while this is truly an amazing movie and certainly in the discussion of best movies ever. It is not perfect. There are flaws within this movie. It is not THE best movie ever made.

Although, when it comes to the visual and digital aspects of the film. It is perfect. The CGI flows seamlessly throughout the movie. It is some of the best special effects I have ever seen on film. The CGI is perfect. No doubt. And when it is mixed with Hans Zimmer's score. It truly is mindblowing. His score is one of the most eerie, memorable, and emotional scores I have ever heard. It perfectly encapsulates the feeling of space and the emotions that come with this interstellar travel. Within the sense of the visuals and score of this movie I have no complaints nor flaws.

When it comes to the acting I also have no complaints. All the actors were relatively great. Matthew McConaughey carries the film immensely. When it comes to characters he is the one we are most emotionally invested in and his story is the one that really matters. Now, there are a lot of characters in this film, and the only other ones you really will care about are Murph and Brand. I wasn't emotionally invested or cared about any other characters so when something happens to them it's like "meh." Also characters make certain decisions where it's like they really did not need to do that. Multiple times on multiple different occasions. For example, Murph burning the cornfield down because her brother wouldn't let her go upstairs. It just isn't necessary. Also the fact that they just don't go to Edmunds planet first.

I thought the film honestly could have potentially been a masterpiece really until the third act. The whole concept of love conquers all and that love is quantifiable was on the brink of being magic. The film follows scientific theories accurately throughout the whole film and then when it comes to tying everything together it does that. They could have made the ending more realistic. And then the scene where McConaughey finally meets his 93 year old daughter again is super underwhelming. That scene had the potential to be one of the most emotional in the entire film and while yes it is still very emotional I feel like if they didn't decide to go with this "love is quantifiable" thing that McConaughey would have had a much better scene. It feels like it ends before it even really begins so with that I was left a little disappointed. I think since they went that route with it that the film might have benefitted with him just being lost in space and not found by space rangers in the end. Way too convenient.

The most emotional scene in the film and honestly my favorite scene is the one where McConaughey watches 23 years worth of family videos. The acting and the score are just superb. Also, there are many scenes that are tense, suspenseful and have you on the edge of your seat. At times it really is wonderful storytelling and filmmaking.

Overall, I think Interstellar is an amazing film. Quite literally very close to being a masterpiece. It really is one of my favorite films of all time and I think everyone should view it at least once. It is also one of the best space movies of all time. The film is super immersive, is visually stunning, and it does have really good story elements; but, some of them are very confusing and for no reason, in my opinion. The script does have some issues, there are some narrative structure problems, and while the ending manages to be somewhat emotional it is overall confusing and underwhelming. The acting is good, but there are some issues with the characters. I think with a few tweaks this film could have been perfect. Although, there are truly some moments of brilliance in this film. It's amazing.

Rating: 9.1 Overall, a movie with brilliant moments and brilliant aspects that is dragged down by its extremely long runtime and slow pace; despite all of this, the movie was great as it explores the relationship between family and profession against the backdrop of a space exploration epic in one of Nolan's finest moments (even though he may falter at times).

Great to Incredible Direction, Good Acting (Good to Very Good from Matthew McConaughey (plays his stereotypical character), Pretty Good from Anne Hathaway (but pretty annoying at times), Good to Very Good from Jessica Chastain, Good from the rest of the cast), Incredible Story, Incredible to Brilliant Screenplay (Symbolism and foreshadowing were carried out very effectively; even though a lot of the science was accurate, the ending was very convoluted), Brilliant Score (Hans Zimmers best work), Incredible to Brilliant Cinematography, Incredible Sound, Incredible Editing, Brilliant Visual Effects, Great Production Design, Pacing was pretty slow and dragged from the story at points; Runtime was very long to the point where past the 1 hour mark a lot of the movie seemed very dragging (About 30 minutes of the movie could be cut/rearranged and the product would have been better), The build to the climax (though very slow and steady) went along very well but the climax itself was extremely convoluted and really made the movie seem very pretentious, The resolution of the film was incredible and emotional as the final 5-10 minutes were some of the best parts of the film; The relationship between Cooper and his daughter was carried out very well as it is a driving force for many of the actions for the character as he has to weigh out his professional and personal obligations.

9.title: A Human Depiction of Space and Time
9.content:
Interstellar is a cinematic spectacle. The film successfully marries powerful existential themes, such as the arrow of time and the nature's indiference towards Man, with utterly beautiful cinematography, a perfect score and good performances. Matthew McConaughey, in particular, is a central part of the film's success as a deep and honest depiction of the human condition.

I would also say that the film is slightly better at portraying the emotional voyage of the crew than its actual scientific aspects. For some viewers, some scenes, such as the ones with Cooper entering the black hole and reaching the singularity, might be a huge turn-off due to their scientific "incorrectness". That being said, the film is not a documentary on Astrophysics and, thus, the emotional experience of entering the unknown should not be jeopardized just because it is fictional. In fact, Interstellar is an emotional journey, more than anything else. Nevertheless, the amount of scientific exposition present in the film does not help to place the emotional side of the story at its centre, and this might make it more difficult to ignore its physically unsound elements. In contrast, a film like 2001: A Space Odyssey leaves much of these details open to interpretation, a reason for which it is more immune to of this sort of criticism. Notwithstanding, the film only falls on physical incoherence in some ocasions because it is also very daring in its depiction of Astrophysical entities which are still very unknown to Mankind, at this point in time. Additionally, these physical incorrect elements are always introduced in service of the plot - Interstellar's visual and sound design of outer space are really out of this world.

In a nutshell, the sheer beauty and emotion of the film, paired with the very human (flawed and often irrational) behaviour of every character makes Interstellar a compelling story and a modern Sci-Fi classic, whose merit lies not only on the gorgeous depiction of the super-human elements of outer space, but also on the depiction of the human interaction with these super-human elements.

9.title: The movie has stayed very close to the story, with minimal efforts to showcase the marvels of space with visual effects

There are movies, which suck you in to their world and leave you mesmerized (like Inception) and then there are movies which leave a higher impression, one of awe and inspiration while passing a message which could define human capability and in ways, humanity itself.

Interstellar, in my view Nolan's attempt at not only creating pioneer cinema, but also communicating to the human urge to get out of our comfort zones n go explore the unknown. In a scene, Mr. Copper (protagonist) shares a trivia with his fellow traveler about many long range yatch drivers not knowing how to swim.

The movie has stayed very close to the story, with minimal efforts to showcase the marvels of space with visual effects (things other Hollywood summer blockbusters can learn from). Some audience may even get a feel of movie being low on budget, at $165mn it's huge enough and patience pays in the second half.

Moving on to story line (without spoilers), is simply about a father keeping his promise to daughter in the backdrop of Earth suffering from famine and an interstellar expedition to find a potential solution.

Performance wise, Mathew is brilliant as the adventurer, explorer, father, son, guide and de facto captain. Sir Caine charms as always, Anne tries and Matt Damon surprises (kept aloof in trailers). Cake however goes to Mackenzie Foy for honest (90%) portrayal of Young Murphy. Both TARS (70% humour) and CASE (100% efficient) are superbly cast too, potential competition for R2D2..

Verdict - Am not eligible to judge such cinema, but I'd recommend you watch it once (if possible in IMAX screen), and wonder whether it's you or the seat which is shaking...Oh, and FYI In physics, three dimensions of space and one of time is the accepted norm. Thank me later ;)

9.title: Stunning on all fronts, a near-masterpiece from Nolan
9.content:
As I sit and write this review, I wonder about the difficulties that one would encounter when attempting to project their dreams and ideas onto paper, better yet onto film. In Interstellar, Christopher Nolan, (along with his frequently less credited brother Johnathan) does so with the beauty and mind-blowing cinematic genius that is 'Interstellar'. Visual effects that do not fall too short of Cuaron's 'Gravity' along with a screenplay of the highest quality (as expected from the Nolan brothers) help to put together what is THE defining sci-fo film of 2014.

I had the pleasure of catching a viewing in IMAX 70MM (highly recommended for this film) at my local media museum and was blown away by the visuals as well as everything that came with it. The movie is set in the not-so-distant future on the backdrop of an earth stricken by what looks to be the adverse effects of global warming. In steps out protagonist in the form of Matthew McConaughey, a NASA pilot-turned-farmer, ready to search the stars and beyond for any sort of hope for mankind. With a run time of 169 minutes, Interstellar is a literally a space odyssey, faintly reminiscent of Kubrick's '2001'. The vast and endless atmosphere and emptiness is incredible and sometimes even frightening to witness on screen. McConaughey puts in a emotion-filled and believable performance and although there wasn't really an outstanding piece of acting, the young Mackenzie Foy put in a heartfelt performance that solidified the on screen father-daughter relationship with McConaughey. Without giving too much of the plot away, this cinematic experience really does open your eyes to the possibilities of human advancements when survival is the only card left to play. The supporting cast are a solid bunch, in the form of the 'Dark Knight Rises' duo Hathaway and Caine. Bill Irwin adds some well needed comic-relief for the voice of the advance assistant with a personality, TARS. Oh, and lest we forget what the genius composer Hans Zimmer contributes. Zimmer's score for this movie may possibly be his best, capturing the emotion, the stress and the fear felt by the characters. These emotions were then transmitted towards the audience in an overwhelming manner. However, what really lifts the film up as 2014's best (if not one of this decade's best) is the idea Nolan presents to his audience; that love transcends past the barriers of time and space as well as a any obstacles set before it. With this he really does create a wonderful piece of film; in essence a sci-fi with the biggest of hearts. No easy feat has been performed here, with different characters' moral compasses spinning this way and that throughout the film, along with the scientific basis is laid out in a not-so-beginner friendly fashion. Fans of popular fiction such as Doctor Who, Donnie Darko shouldn't find the concepts difficult to grasp. However not everyone falls under this bracket. Moreover, the pacing fluctuates throughout the movie and there are times where some characters' actions and motives can seem silly and questionable. Interstellar is not a perfect film, and perhaps not Nolan's greatest either, however what it is, is a jaw-dropping voyage into the unknown as well as the human heart, and is most definitely the director's most grandeur outing. 9.5/10

9.title: Interstellar: A Symphony of Science, Spectacle, and Heart
9.content:
Embark on a mind-bending odyssey through the vast, uncharted reaches of space in Christopher Nolan's awe-inspiring masterpiece, Interstellar. Bathed in the ethereal glow of Hans Zimmer's haunting score, this cinematic tour de force delves into the mysteries of the cosmos with both scientific rigor and unbridled awe.

Witness the breathtaking spectacle of a wormhole, a gateway to distant galaxies teeming with the promise of new worlds. Experience the visceral thrill of hurtling through the universe, the awe-inspiring vastness of space dwarfing the human existence. Brace yourself for the chilling reality of a dying Earth, a stark reminder of the fragility of our own planet.

But Interstellar is more than just a visual feast. It's a poignant exploration of the human condition, a testament to the enduring power of love and family in the face of overwhelming odds. Matthew McConaughey delivers a masterful performance as Cooper, a conflicted father grappling with the agonizing choice between his mission and his yearning for his daughter.

Prepare to be drawn into the intricate web of theoretical physics and philosophical questions woven into the narrative. Ponder the nature of time and space, the possibility of extraterrestrial life, and the enduring human quest for answers to the universe's greatest mysteries.

Interstellar is a cinematic experience that reaches for the stars, challenging our perception of reality and igniting our sense of wonder. 9.title: A Cinematic Masterpiece That Transcends Time and Space
9.content:
When Interstellar first graced the silver screen, it wasn't just a film-it was an experience that stretched the boundaries of our imagination. Christopher Nolan's ambitious exploration of love, time, and the vast mysteries of the cosmos is a cinematic triumph that resonates deeply, even upon multiple viewings.

The recent theatrical re-release offered a fresh opportunity to dive back into this intricate tapestry of interstellar travel and human emotion. It also sparked intriguing "what-if" scenarios that add even more layers to an already complex narrative. One can't help but wonder: What if Cooper and his crew had bypassed Dr. Mann's planet and headed straight to Edmunds' world?

In this alternate storyline, the crew avoids the treacherous deceptions on Mann's icy wasteland. Instead, they discover Edmunds' planet to be not just habitable but a welcoming new home-a beacon of hope realized sooner. The challenges that consumed precious time and resources are sidestepped, allowing humanity's new chapter to begin without the costly detours.

However, this seemingly fortunate path comes with a profound cost. Without the slingshot maneuver around Gargantua, Cooper and TARS never enter the tesseract. The pivotal exchange of quantum data-that bridge between dimensions enabling Murph to solve the gravity equation-never occurs. The information remains forever "beyond the horizon," inaccessible and enigmatic. As a result, Plan A, the rescue of Earth's remaining population, fades into oblivion.

Cooper might have had enough fuel to return to Earth sooner, potentially reuniting with Murph without the burden of decades lost. Yet, without the critical data, his homecoming would be bittersweet-a hero returning with empty hands to a dying world. The people of Earth, including his beloved daughter, face inevitable extinction. The irony is heart-wrenching: while humanity's legacy takes root light-years away on Edmunds' planet, the very individuals who fought valiantly for its survival are left behind.

This scenario opens a Pandora's box of ethical and philosophical dilemmas. Is the survival of our species justified if it means sacrificing the very people who embody its essence? The new civilization on Edmunds' planet would grow isolated from Earth's rich tapestry of cultures, histories, and beliefs. With only a handful of pioneers and limited knowledge, society would develop along a singular narrative. Their creation story centers on an exodus from a dying planet-a tale of survival stripped of the nuances that millennia of human experience have woven.

This lack of cultural and religious plurality could lead to a society with vastly different values. Would they foster a unity born from shared origins, or would new divisions and belief systems arise over time? History suggests that the human spirit naturally seeks meaning, potentially giving birth to new myths and traditions despite the initial absence of Earth's diverse heritage.

Moreover, bypassing Mann's planet eliminates critical character arcs and themes. Dr. Mann represents the darker facets of human nature-the fear, desperation, and selfishness that can emerge in extreme circumstances. His actions serve as a stark contrast to the selflessness displayed by Cooper and his crew. Without this confrontation, the narrative loses a vital exploration of moral ambiguity and the resilience of the human spirit under duress.

The time dilation near Gargantua also plays a pivotal role in the original story, emphasizing the relentless and unforgiving nature of time-especially in relation to love and loss. By avoiding Gargantua, the emotional weight of missed decades and the visual representation of time as a tangible force are diminished. The story shifts focus, becoming less about the interplay between time and human relationships and more about the immediate consequences of choice.

Yet, this alternate take doesn't diminish the film's core questions-it magnifies them. What responsibilities do we bear when making decisions that affect not just ourselves but the entirety of humanity? Is the preservation of human life enough, or is there intrinsic value in the collective experiences and histories that define us?

Christopher Nolan's Interstellar masterfully navigates these complex themes, and such thought experiments only deepen our appreciation for his work. The film doesn't just tell a story; it invites us to ponder our place in the universe, the ties that bind us, and the lengths we're willing to go to secure a future for generations to come.

In conclusion, Interstellar isn't just a sci-fi adventure; it's a profound meditation on existence. Whether considering the film as it stands or exploring alternate narratives, it's clear that its impact is enduring. It challenges and inspires, reminding us that while the cosmos is vast and indifferent, the human capacity for love, sacrifice, and hope remains our most potent force.

9.title: A Timeless Film
9.content:
Director Christopher Nolan's science fiction film Interstellar evinces wonder at the spectacles of the cosmos and, equally, terror at the unceasing power and indifference of the forces of nature.

In his imposing and visionary journey across space, Nolan has us encounter time in a headfirst way. From the methodical sounds of a metronome dinning to how the film's titular spacecraft revolves with a slow clockwise spin in the deep expanse of space, the film doesn't fight to give away the fact that time is a prominent theme. However, why is time so ultimately moving here?

CA Zamora, Thomas CEEB: 111273 Fall 2023 10 FY RD CAID: 31926013 In a film that grounds its narrative in science, Nolan demonstrates that time isn't purely cosmological but human. The experience of the dilation of time across space isn't truly as remote as it looks but is deeply analogous to the loss of time in our lives. As Tom Linden described, "for those stuck in places for years or serving on a mission overseas, coming home is rarely so much about the spatial element as it's about the passage of time-it is the realization that life has moved on in our absence". Ultimately, the recognition that we aren't always in control of our lives.

However, despite the sorrow of being trapped within the relentless forces of nature, Interstellar offers us resistance against time; time cannot be stopped, yet it can be transcended.

After Cooper sacrifices himself, descending into the black hole to save humanity, he approaches the singularity. Inside the singularity, through a higher spatial dimension, Cooper discovers he can move freely outside of the flow of time. Despite this, however, Cooper is still restricted from communicating with his daughter until he exerts a force across space-time, bringing him and Murph together from across the universe. It is described that this force is gravity; however, Nolan demonstrates that, ultimately, it is the force of his enduring love for Murph that allows Cooper to unite with her after 75 years.

At the film's crux, Interstellar suggests that our experience with love allows us to transcend time-as the force of love is timeless. Whether through artifacts, books, words, images, language, pictures, stories, or morse code written at the nucleus of a black hole, the physical incarnations of our love are how we can impute a force across time.

Transcending time is holding onto our old knowledge, wisdom, and sentiment tenaciously; it is empathizing with those who haven't even been born yet. It's to keep the love of a father alive while he is stuck in your past, spreading it to others in the present and rediscovering it in the future.

9.title: The Final Frontier
9.content: Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" is perhaps his most ambitious and beautiful looking film to date. More importantly, it may be his more heartfelt. The stakes are very high in this movie with mankind being on the verge of extinction due to a new Dust Bowl. Food has become so precious that farmers have become more valuable than engineers. Matthew McConaughey as the protagonist Cooper, a former astronaut laments how mankind as become caretakers instead of explorers. He is eventually called by Professor Brand (Michael Caine), who runs a secret NASA installation, to explore a possible chance for mankind's survival. In doing so he must travel to a wormhole near Saturn for a habitable environment for humans. In this tension to save humanity, the relationship between Cooper and his daughter serves as a microcosm. The day before he leaves they share a scene where the Murphy the daughter resents Cooper for abandoning her. This could have been very manipulative and sappy in another movie however this came of as real and emotional due to the actor's performances. Speaking of which, Matthew McConaughey gives another outstanding performance in his film, who is able to handle the heavy emotions required. Take a scene where he is watching a video feed of his son. Many years have passed on Earth while Cooper and his crew are in space. His son is now showing him his child and is catching him up on what has gone on in his life. How McConaughey reacts to this is absolutely touching and makes the audience care about these characters. The movie has an excellent supporting cast that includes Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain (as a grown up Murphy), and another A- list celebrity whose name is nowhere in the credits because I assume the filmmakers wanted it to be a surprise. There are also some very interesting robot characters, that have one of the most original designs I've ever seen. The movie is an absolute joyful experience to watch, and provides visuals of space this side of "Gravity". In a film where CGI is basically mandatory, Nolan manages to use a little as possible. Apparently he even shot these scenes WITHOUT ANY GREEN SCREENS!!! There are scenes on an ice planet that could have been very convenient to use green screen, yet it was actually filmed on a glacier in Iceland. To top it off Hans Zimmer backs it up with arguably the best score of his career and that's saying something. "2001: A Space Odyssey" is supposed the film that inspired Christopher Nolan and that definitely shows. Although Stanley's Kubrick's film lacks the emotional touch of "Interstellar". I would not be surprised if Nolan owes a debt to Andrei Tartovsky's "Solaris", a sci-fi epic that deals with the emotional turmoil of the characters while raising questions about humanity. In this review I have left out countless point points and twists, because this movie is more of an experience than a formulaic picture. Unlike Nolan's recent films, this was not released as a summer blockbuster and I can see why. This is perhaps his most thought-provoking film, even more so than "Inception". The reason I give this movie a 9/10 instead of a perfect score is that I often felt that there was too much scientific speak in the dialogue, though granted it is delivered well by the actors. However the flaws are really just nitpicks. One final comment is that while for the first 2/3 of the movie I was admiring the visuals, the final act made me lean forward in my seat, with my mouth dropped.

9.title: A beautiful, ambitious, fascinating odyssey.
9.content:
I saw Interstellar this weekend, as did many people. I have a lot to talk about in regards to this film, so let me begin.

I have to start off by saying.... wow. Just, wow. What an absolutely mesmerizing film. I know it's cliché to say, but I don't think I've ever seen anything quite like it. In recent decades, anyway. The visual effects and cinematography are nothing less than utterly fantastic, I could've sworn that they actually filmed the space scenes out in space. They're that good. As others have said, there's an emotional core to the plot that makes the three hour ride so worthwhile, and it's what makes the film so different from what Nolan usually tackles. The cast gives uniformly great performances, but one I have to particularly point out because hot damn did he do one heck of a job in it was Matthew McConaughey. If he doesn't get at least a Best Actor nomination at the Oscars next year, heads will roll. The writing in the film is also overall a wonder, perfectly mixing emotion, drama, and even some funny bits here in there. The score by Hans Zimmer is actually a step up from his recent works, and accompanies the film greatly with the use of quiet, eerie melodies and loud, satisfying crescendos. (I even think I noticed a few 2001 references in there, but it's probably just me!)

Interstellar is Christopher Nolan's most personal work. This is where at he's his most human, and his most beautiful. This is a work of art, a piece of cerebral science fiction and a heart-pounding drama that is truly special in its own way. It's refreshingly unusual, to the point where it asks us, the audience to be willing to understand it: a story of family, finding new frontiers, loss, the longing to see a loved one's face again. The film in general in some ways actually hankered me back to an ever so popular comparison, 2001: A Space Odyssey and even last year's sci-fi drama, Gravity, due to the huge technical milestones both had pioneered. Steven Soderbergh's little-seen and not that well-regarded remake of Solaris from 2002 is also eerily similar to this in many regards, but this is the film Solaris should have been. But whatever, time for me to stop rambling and get back onto my thoughts with this film.

Many aren't going like Interstellar, and write it off as a pretentious, overlong hodgepodge with no real worth. Or, they'll see it for the fascinating, complex film it actually is. It's bound to be one of the most controversial films of this decade, this century if my sights aren't too ludicrous. There's a reason why this movie is getting such a highly divided reception among critics. It's thrown them off, they weren't expecting such a film on a almost mindbogglingly huge scale with so many underlying messages to it. I've seen quite a lot of people slam the almost three hour long running time, but me? I couldn't take my eyes of the screen for a second, I was completely riveted.

Interstellar is a simply stunning work, and one of (if not the best) films of 2014. It's a lot of things: emotional, moving, visceral, powerful and most of all staggeringly ambitious. It's one heck of an experience, whether you end up loving or hating it, that will stay in your mind one way or another. To say that this film may be Nolan's masterpiece isn't that far of a stretch, despite all the excellent films on his repertoire. If your theater has IMAX, PLEASE watch it in that format. It's the definitive way to see the film.

My point is, go see it. Now. Films like these are a rarity nowadays.

Bravo, Nolan. Film was invented for creations like this.

9.title: A Modern Sci-Fi Classic That Stands the Test of Time

Christopher Nolan's Interstellar has rightfully earned its place as one of the greatest sci-fi films of the modern era. A decade after its release, it remains an awe-inspiring cinematic experience, blending breathtaking visuals, emotional storytelling, and mind-bending scientific concepts into an unforgettable journey.

The film's scope is immense, yet it never loses sight of its heart-the human connections that drive the story. Matthew McConaughey delivers a career-defining performance as Cooper, making his struggle both deeply personal and universally relatable. The supporting cast, including Anne Hathaway and Jessica Chastain, adds further depth to the narrative, ensuring that every moment carries weight.

Visually, Interstellar is a masterpiece. The stunning depictions of space, wormholes, and alien planets are as beautiful as they are scientifically intriguing. Combined with Hans Zimmer's powerful and haunting score, the film becomes an immersive experience that lingers long after the credits roll.

While some of the plot's complexities might require multiple viewings to fully grasp, that only adds to its rewatch value. The twists and turns keep the audience engaged, leading to an emotional and thought-provoking conclusion that solidifies Interstellar as a true sci-fi epic.

It's a must-watch for anyone who loves intelligent, ambitious storytelling. Though not without minor flaws, its impact is undeniable-an instant classic that continues to inspire and amaze.

9.title: Interstellar

Interstellar, directed by Christopher Nolan in 2014, is a masterpiece of science fiction. As someone who has watched it, I find the film captivating both emotionally and scientifically. Starring Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, and Jessica Chastain, it explores profound themes centered around the survival of humanity and a father-daughter relationship.

The film stands out with its intricate narrative combining concepts of time, space, gravity, and human emotions. Its visual effects, accompanied by Hans Zimmer's iconic score, truly take you to the edges of the universe. Moreover, its foundation in real science (for instance, the depiction of the black hole created with guidance from physicist Kip Thorne) sets it apart from other movies in its genre.

However, the film's greatest strength lies in blending cold scientific concepts with a warm human story. It raises thought-provoking questions, such as, "Could love be the only force that transcends dimensions in the universe?" This gives it the feel of a story about existence rather than just science fiction. The emotional intensity between Cooper and Murph, especially in the final scenes, is deeply moving.

9.title: A new age cinematic masterpiece
9.content:
After realizing the severity of Earth's critical condition, a team of scientists, explorers, and pioneers rush through space on an expedition to find an inhabitable planet.

Christopher Nolan's imagination and ideas come in handfuls with this magical, intense, sci-fi rollercoaster. This is a new-age Odyssey, and if that isn't reason enough to see this film than I don't know what is. Everything needed in a breathtaking film is displayed throughout 169 minutes and takes cinema to a new level. Firstly, the soundtrack is phenomenal. Hans Zimmer is of course brilliant in this film and his work matches the film in every way, only adding to the experiences and emotions. As the film deepens and intensifies, so does Hans' score and as the movie ends, we hear the tense yet hopeful melody that the film has been building up to. Even more sullen and dark moments have Hans Zimmer all over them with darkening tones. Next is Nolan's visual effects. This film has beautiful scenes and cinematography that encompasses the entire film. Hoyte Van Hoytema, the director of cinematography, is a master and his work on this film is incredible. His work can be seen in other notable films, such as Her (2013), Ad Astra (2019), and Dunkirk (2017). And of course, the direction. Nolan shows some of his best work in this film, showing the perfect angles and knowing exactly where to cut to each character and scene to match Hans Zimmer's astonishing scores.

A prominent theme in this movie is gravity, not only scientifically, but metaphorically too, such as the gravity the characters feel, and the gravity we feel along with them through the direction of the film, and incredible acting. Matthew McConaughey does exceptional work here, along with supporting actress Anne Hathaway, who's chemistry in this film are both amazing and believable. I can't imagine the main character being anyone else other than Matthew McConaughey, seeing as he himself was basically the entire movie. His performance was incredibly moving and heartfelt, I felt like I could feel his every thought and emotion.

The film's plot in itself is a confusing one, where questions are raised, then answered, and raise more questions. This is meticulously designed by Nolan, as his films typically are. However, one thing is clear, so to speak. This is that love is a strong force in our universe, as is gravity. Like, gravity, love will gravitate us towards those we love. Love is not itself something we can explain or comprehend, and it being a driving force for us is unexplainable, yet incredibly powerful. Such as Brand felt her move stretch across galaxies for her fellow scientist and explorer, our love for the ones we truly do love will stretch as far as possible and grows as the distance between them grows as well.

Some of this film will remain a mystery, as will the fate and future of humanity, but like with the mystery of love, and how it will grow and stretch no matter the distance, humanity will remain ever expanding and searching for its next place in the universe, physically and symbolically.

9.title: A breathtaking journey through space, time and emotion
9.content:
Interstellar is one of those rare films that manages to combine hard science fiction with deeply human emotion in a way that few others can. Christopher Nolan delivers a cinematic experience that is both intellectually stimulating and emotionally profound.

The film's visuals are absolutely stunning - from the vastness of space to the haunting beauty of distant planets, every frame feels meticulously crafted. Hans Zimmer's powerful, organ-driven score elevates the experience to an almost spiritual level, perfectly complementing the film's themes of isolation, love, and survival.

Matthew McConaughey gives one of the strongest performances of his career as Cooper, bringing genuine warmth and depth to a character torn between duty and love. The supporting cast, especially Anne Hathaway and Jessica Chastain, are equally compelling, adding layers of complexity to the story.

What truly sets Interstellar apart is its ambition. It dares to explore complex scientific concepts - relativity, black holes, time dilation - while never losing sight of the emotional core: a father's love for his daughter. Yes, some moments may stretch plausibility, and the ending remains divisive for some, but the overall impact is undeniable.

It's not a perfect film, but it's a bold, beautiful, and thought-provoking one. Interstellar is the kind of movie that stays with you long after the credits roll - not just because of what you saw, but because of what you felt. A modern sci-fi masterpiece.
